```{r, set up}
#| echo: FALSE

library(tidyverse)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(performance)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

```

```{r, dataset setup}
#| echo: FALSE

# Data loading

data("NMES1988")

data <- NMES1988

# Selecting my variables of interest 

data <- data |>
  select(visits, chronic, health, gender, school, insurance) |> 

#Assigning reference groups of Men and Single
  
  mutate(
    health = fct_relevel(factor(health), "average"),
    gender = fct_relevel(factor(gender), "male"),
    insurance = fct_relevel(factor(insurance), "no")
  )

```

The `NMES1988` data describe 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. It details several variables with the outcome variable being number of physician office visits. The rest are listed below

| Variable    | Description                                                |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `visits`    | **Outcome:** physician office visits between 1987 and 1988 |
| `chronic`   | Number of chronic conditions                               |
| `health`    | Self-perceived health: `poor`, `average`, or `excellent`   |
| `gender`    | `male` of `female`                                         |
| `school`    | Years of education                                         |
| `insurance` | Covered by private insurance: `no` or `yes`                |

Reference groups are **Average** health, **Male**, and **No** insurance.


```{r describe}
#| echo: FALSE

# Describe the data

visits_summary <- data |>
  summarise(
    n      = n(),
    mean   = mean(visits),
    var    = var(visits),
    p_zero = mean(visits == 0),
    max    = max(visits)
  )

# making it a proper table
gt(visits_summary)

```

```{r descriptive plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Creating a plot of the overall distribution of the outcome variable (number of visits)
descriptive_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of visits", y = "Number of People")

descriptive_plot

```

The visits outcome **is a count.** Whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed. **The variance (`r round(visits_summary$var, 2)`) is about `r round(visits_summary$var / visits_summary$mean, 2)` times the mean (`r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`).** **`r round(100 * visits_summary$p_zero)`% of people had no visits.** The greatest number of visits reported **(`r round(visits_summary$max, 2)`)**is a shockingly large number, but could be legitimate. 

```{r, gaussian model test}
#| echo: FALSE

# Fiting a Gaussian model

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity")
)

#simulation 
set.seed(500)
res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(m_gauss, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_gauss)

```


A linear model is a poor choice for the visits outcome variable because the visits data are counts, meaning that negative visits and half visits are impossible/meaningless values. This is evidenced by the DHARMa simulations. The residuals, shown in the QQ plot, do not follow the expected flat diagonal line. The outlier and KS tests also speak to this concern. In the residual-vs-predicted plot, as the predicted probability approaches 1, the distribution becomes more compressed toward the lower end of residual values. This is also evidenced by the red 0.5 quantile line. Taken together, its clear these data are not a good fit for a Gaussian model. 


```{r poisson null}
#| echo: FALSE

# Null (intercept-only) Poisson model: no predictors
null <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# One-predictor Poisson model: Does having a chronic condition predict visit counts?
chronic_pred <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))


# Full Poisson model: all five predictors at once. Chronic, health, gender, school, insurance explain additional variation. 
full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

```


```{r, anova tests}
#| echo: FALSE

tests <- anova(null, chronic_pred, full)

```

```{r, prepare tests}
#| echo: FALSE

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

```

```{r, extract model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(null)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(chronic_pred)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(full)

```

```{r, combine model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Chronic_pred",
  "M2: Full")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2)
```

```{r, combine comparisons}
#| echo: FALSE

comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)

```

```{r, model comparison table}
#| echo: FALSE

comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

```

For the comparison between M0 and M1, nested χ² = 2,175.428, p <.001. For the comparison between M1 and M2, nested χ² = 959.924, p <.001. Both of these likelihood-ratio tests indicate a statistically significant improvement in model fit. This means that adding the additional predictors improved the model fit across both comparisons, suggesting that M2 is a better fit model than M1 and M0. Further, the AIC and BIC decreased for both comparisons, once again implying that M2 is a good model to select. For these reasons, I have selected M2 as the ideal model.  

```{r, select model}
#| echo: FALSE

selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "M0: Null" = null,
  "M1: Chronic_pred" = chronic_pred,
  "M2: Full" = full,
  )

```

The provisionally selected model is **`r selected_name`**.

Its performance is:

- AIC = **`r round(AIC(selected_model), 3)`**
- BIC = **`r round(BIC(selected_model), 3)`**

```{r poisson dharma}
#| echo: FALSE

# Seed was always set to 500 for this whole document. 
set.seed(500)

# Simulates 500 new datasets from the fitted full poisson model.
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(full, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

#  QQ plot and residuals vs. predicted values
plot(res_pois)

```
```{r, pois-dispersion}
#| echo: FALSE

# Dispersion test

disp_pois <- testDispersion(res_pois)
disp_pois

```

```{r, poisson zeros}
#| echo: FALSE

# Zero-inflation test

zi_pois <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)
zi_pois

```


The DHARMa plots suggest that the Poisson model is a poor fit. The dispersion ratio is `r round(disp_pois$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_pois$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_pois$p.value, 3)))`), and there are `r round(zi_pois$statistic, 2)` times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows. 

The over dispersion observed here matters because it means that the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean has been violated. In this case the variance is underestimated, meaning that model's standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the *p*-values are too small. I would not move straight to a zero-inflated model based on this zero-inflation test alone because the test only tells me that there are more zeros than the Poisson expects, it does not tell me if these zeros are coming from structural reasons (i.e. some people have no reason to visit a doctor during this period). Whether the zeros are structural or not will define if I should move to a  zero-inflated model. 

```{r, nb}
#| echo: FALSE

# Negative binomial (NB2) model
neg_binom <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)

summary(neg_binom)

# LRT
lrt_nb<-anova(full, neg_binom)
lrt_nb

```

The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) = `r round(lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"], 2)`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`.

This test has 1 degree of freedom because the negative binomial model adds more more layer of complexity by adding one parameter that describes the extra variability in the data. Yes, the  NB2 fit significantly better than the Poisson. This is evidenced by the large reduction in AIC and BIC and the significance of the LRT test. This tells us that adding complexity to the model didn't take away from the significance of the relationship. The NB2 resolved our over dispersion issue, but our issue of excess zero may remain. 


```{r, nb-dharma}
#| echo: FALSE

# Same seed as before

set.seed(500)

# If the NB is adequate, these should now be uniform, unlike the Poisson's.
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(neg_binom, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# QQ plot: points should now sit close to the diagonal.
# Residuals vs. predicted: should be roughly flat.
plot(res_nb)

```

```{r, nb-tests}
#| echo: FALSE

disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)

# Zero inflation
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)

```

The NB resolved the over dispersion: the dispersion ratio is now `r round(disp_nb$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_nb$p.value, 3)))`), close to 1 and non-significant.

```{r nb-pred-plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Predicted mean visit counts from the additive NB, on the count scale.
# "chronic [0:20]" plots chronic conditions from 0 to 20.

pred_nb <- predict_response(neg_binom, terms = "chronic [0:20]")

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted visit counts by number of chronic conditions",
    x     = "Chronic conditions", y = "Predicted visits"
  )

```

The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors because of the the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, multiplying the expected count, so the same one-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

# Part 5: Do the zeros need their own model?

Given that my NB2 zero-inflation test produced a significant result, I will test ZINB
and Hurdle NB models to see if the fit is improved and the zero-inflation is resolved. 


```{r zero-models}
#| echo: FALSE
#| eval: false

# Zero-inflated NB with a constant zero-inflation probability
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ 1,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Zero-inflated NB with predictors in the zero part
m_zinb_full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Hurdle NB
m_hurd <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2()
)

# Compare models
anova(neg_binom, m_zinb_full)

# The hurdle isn't nested in the NB, so compare with AIC/BIC (lower = better)
AIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
BIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)

# Then re-check the chosen model with DHARMa
set.seed(500)
res_zinb <- simulateResiduals(m_zinb_full, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
testZeroInflation(res_zinb)


```
